notes.front: What is the operating maneuvering speed (VO)?
notes.back: The maximum speed at which, at any given weight, full control deflection will not exceed the design limit load factor.
notes.explanation: It is a historical operating limitation that applies only to certain airplanes, alongside or instead of VA.
notes.example: Like VA, but stated as a limit that holds at any weight, and found only in some airplanes' manuals.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: VO is a historical operating limitation applicable to certain airplanes only. It represents the maximum speed where, at any given weight, the pilot may apply full control excursion without exceeding the design limit load factor.

notes.front: Which stalls count as accelerated manoeuvre stalls?
notes.back: Any stall that occurs when the G-load is greater than +1G.
notes.explanation: At +1G a given airplane stalls at the same indicated airspeed; extra G raises that speed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: Stalls encountered any time the G-load exceeds +1G are called “accelerated maneuver stalls.”

notes.front: Can an airplane stall at a higher indicated airspeed than its published stall speed?
notes.back: Yes: when accelerated above +1G, such as in a turn, a pull-up or another abrupt change of flightpath.
notes.explanation: Published stall speeds assume +1G, steady, unaccelerated flight.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: the airplane can also stall at a higher indicated airspeed when the airplane is subject to an acceleration greater than +1G, such as when turning, pulling up, or other abrupt changes in flightpath.

notes.front: What are two situations in which an accelerated stall most often happens inadvertently?
notes.back: Any two of: improperly executed turns, stall and spin recoveries, pullouts from steep dives, overshooting a base-to-final turn.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that an accelerated stall is typically demonstrated during steep turns.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: The accelerated stall would most frequently occur inadvertently during improperly executed turns, stall and spin recoveries, pullouts from steep dives, or when overshooting a base to final turn.

notes.front: Recovering from a steep dive, a pilot pulls hard and the airplane stalls at 85 knots, though its published stall speed is 55 knots. What has happened?
notes.back: An accelerated stall: the G-load above +1G raised the stall speed.
notes.explanation: Pullouts from steep dives are a typical setting, and a stall above +1G can come at a higher indicated airspeed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: The accelerated stall would most frequently occur inadvertently during improperly executed turns, stall and spin recoveries, pullouts from steep dives, or when overshooting a base to final turn.

notes.front: Who may be required to perform or demonstrate an accelerated stall on a practical test?
notes.back: Only commercial pilot and flight instructor applicants.
notes.explanation: All pilots should still know the situations that cause one, how to recognise it and how to recover.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: This is a maneuver only commercial pilot and flight instructor applicants may be required to perform or demonstrate on a practical test.

notes.front: Why should accelerated stalls never be practised with the flaps extended?
notes.back: The design G-load limits are lower in that configuration.
notes.explanation: An accelerated stall is flown above +1G, and the G limits with flaps extended are lower.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: A pilot should never practice accelerated stalls with wing flaps in the extended position due to the lower design G-load limitations in that configuration.

notes.front: Preparing for the commercial test, a friend suggests practising accelerated stalls with 20° of flap "to keep the speeds low". What do you say?
notes.back: No: practise them with the flaps up.
notes.explanation: Flaps extended bring lower design G-load limits, and the handbook says never to practise accelerated stalls that way.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: A pilot should never practice accelerated stalls with wing flaps in the extended position due to the lower design G-load limitations in that configuration.

notes.front: What bank and what maximum speed does the handbook give for practising accelerated stalls?
notes.back: About 45° of bank, never faster than the manufacturer's recommended speed, VA or VO.
notes.explanation: The commercial test likewise uses a coordinated 45° turn with airspeed not above VA.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: Accelerated stalls should be performed with a bank of approximately 45°, and in no case at a speed greater than the airplane manufacturer’s recommended airspeed, or the specified design maneuvering speed (VA) or operating maneuvering speed (VO).

notes.front: Why must accelerated stalls not be flown above VA or VO?
notes.back: Above them the airplane can reach its design load limit before the critical angle of attack, so it can be overstressed.
notes.explanation: At or below VA or VO the wing stalls, which unloads it, before the design load limit is reached.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: At speeds above VA or VO, the airplane can reach its design load limit at less than the critical AOA. This condition makes it possible to add additional load and overstress the airplane.

notes.front: You roll into a coordinated 45° turn at 120 knots to demonstrate an accelerated stall; VA is 105 knots. When may you start increasing the angle of attack to the stall?
notes.back: Only once the airspeed has slowed to VA (and is 5 to 10 percent above the unaccelerated stall speed).
notes.explanation: The handbook allows entry above VA only if the pilot waits for the speed to decay before loading the wing.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: Alternatively, the pilot rolls the airplane into a coordinated, level-flight 45° turn at an airspeed above VA or VO. After the airspeed slows to VA or VO, and at an airspeed 5 to 10 percent faster than the unaccelerated stall speed, the pilot progressively increases the AOA

notes.front: How does an accelerated stall in a coordinated turn differ from one in an uncoordinated turn?
notes.back: Coordinated: the nose pitches away as both wings stall nearly together. Uncoordinated: the bank angle may change.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the uncoordinated stall behaviour may include a bank change until the angle of attack is reduced.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: If the airplane is not properly coordinated at the time of stall, the stall behavior may include a change in bank angle until the AOA has been reduced.

notes.front: Why can stalls from abrupt manoeuvres surprise an inexperienced pilot?
notes.back: They occur at higher-than-normal airspeeds or lower-than-expected pitch attitudes, and are more aggressive than +1G stalls.
notes.explanation: Failing to recover at once may lead to a spin or another departure from controlled flight.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: Stalls that result from abrupt maneuvers tend to be more aggressive than unaccelerated +1G stalls. Because they occur at higher-than-normal airspeeds or may occur at lower-than-anticipated pitch attitudes, they can surprise an inexperienced pilot.

notes.front: Which stall speed should the pilot know before performing an accelerated stall?
notes.back: The published stall speed for 45° of bank, flaps up.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes that this speed is typically published in the airplane flight manual.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 5 "Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training", "Accelerated Stalls"
notes.evidence: The pilot should know the published stall speed for 45° of bank, flaps up, before performing the maneuver.

notes.front: On the commercial test, the accelerated stall entry altitude must let the task finish no lower than {{c1::3,000 feet}} above ground level.
notes.explanation: After recovery the task also asks for a climb at VX or VY and a return to the altitude the evaluator specifies.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation VII, Task D "Accelerated Stalls", CA.VII.D.S2
notes.evidence: Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On the commercial test, how is the accelerated stall entered?
notes.back: From a coordinated 45° turn, increasing elevator back pressure smoothly and firmly until an impending stall.
notes.explanation: Power is set so the airspeed does not exceed VA or another flight manual limit.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation VII, Task D "Accelerated Stalls", CA.VII.D.S4 and S5
notes.evidence: Establish and maintain a coordinated turn in a 45° bank, increasing elevator back pressure smoothly and firmly until an impending stall is reached.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On the commercial test, does the Spin Awareness task require the applicant to fly a spin?
notes.back: No: it tests knowledge and risk management only; its skills section is left blank.
notes.explanation: The task covers spin causes, phases and the recovery procedure as knowledge.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation VII, Task E "Spin Awareness"
notes.evidence: Skills: The applicant exhibits the skill to: [Intentionally left blank].
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force
